USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold firm within the 90-day truce and pursue the negotiation hard, but do not escalate. Keep the Jan 1 List 3 hike suspended and push China to deliver on concrete structural concessions and farm purchases, using the tariffs already in place (~$250B) as leverage rather than ratcheting them up. Manage the Huawei/Meng and detained-Canadians issue carefully so the hostage standoff does not torpedo the talks or alienate Canada.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is moderate, not existential. US fundamentals remain solid (consumer sentiment ~98.3, industrial production rising, CPI ~2%), so the dispute is not yet cratering the broader economy. But the costs are real and concentrated: soybean exports to China are down roughly 94-97% and 2018 is the worst farm-income year since 2002 (period-press reports), a domestic political and economic pressure point; markets are fragile (10Y yield fell from ~3.2% to 2.77%, WTI collapsed from ~$75 to ~$46, and the Dow swung ~800 points on the Meng news); and the Dec 1 Meng Wanzhou arrest plus China's Dec 10 detention of two Canadians is an unplanned escalation that threatens the truce agreed at the G20 and strains ally cohesion with Canada. This is material GDP/farm drag and domestic political pressure (roughly the +0.5 'high' anchor, tempered by the fact the US holds the initiative and the truce is intact), hence +0.35. Action-wise, the US still holds leverage and the 90-day window is the right vehicle to extract concessions on IP/tech-transfer and reopen the farm market, so escalation (breaking the truce to 25%) would hurt US farmers and markets precisely when China is already withholding soybean purchases; maximal concession would squander leverage. Thus a hold/negotiate stance at +0.1 is appropriate.
key_factors: 90-day G20 truce intact (Dec 1); Jan 1 tariff hike suspended
US farm belt badly hurt: soybean exports to China down 94-97%, worst farm income since 2002
Fragile markets: 10Y yield 3.2%->2.77%, WTI ~$75->$46, Dow swing ~800 pts
Meng Wanzhou arrest (Dec 1) + China detaining 2 Canadians (Dec 10) threaten truce and Canada ties
US macro solid: sentiment ~98, IP up, CPI ~2%, but Fed tightening to 2.27%

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires: Trump and Xi agree to 90-day negotiation window; planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% suspended. Same day Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
China detains Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor, widely viewed as retaliation for the Meng arrest.
US soybean sales to China down 94% thanks to Trump trade war.
China didn't restart buying soybeans after truce; Farm Bureau estimates soybean exports to China down 97% this year; 2018 worst net farm income since 2002.
10Y yield fell from ~3.2% (early Oct) to 2.77% (Dec 19), a sharp risk-off move.
WTI fell from ~$75 to ~$46 by mid-December, signaling growth concerns.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain the G20 90-day truce and negotiate seriously within it, seeking to lock in the postponement of the List 3 10%-to-25% tariff increase while pressing for the release of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou and a broader de-escalation — handling the Huawei/Canadian-detainee matter through diplomacy and leverage rather than trade escalation. Do not retaliate on tariffs now, because blowing up the truce would trigger the January 1 hike to 25% on ~$200B of exports at a moment when our economy is already decelerating.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high and firm-level: the US already has ~$250B of our exports under tariff (25% on $50B + 10% on ~$200B), and the December 1 arrest of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou in Canada on US extradition is direct firm-level targeting of our flagship tech champion with a widening hostage dimension (we detained Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor on Dec 10, widely read as retaliation). This sits at the +0.5 CHN anchor and arguably above it. Macro confirms the dispute is biting: Q3 GDP was 6.5% — slowest since early 2009 — and November industrial production growth eased to 5.4%, its lowest since 2009, with export growth halving and the yuan down ~6% this year, which is why I score 0.55 rather than lower. However, it is not existential because a 90-day truce is in force — the Jan 1 escalation is suspended, both sides committed to talks, and our economy is still growing ~6.5% with policy space (RRR cuts). On action, escalation is the wrong move: a tariff war is asymmetric, hitting our larger export base far harder than US imports from us, and would immediately endanger the suspended tariff hike. The disciplined path is hold-and-negotiate — convert the truce into a durable deal that removes the 25% threat, and use our leverage (the detained Canadians) mainly to force de-escalation on Huawei rather than to widen the conflict. That justifies a mildly de-escalatory action stance of +0.2 and a 'negotiate' posture.
key_factors: 90-day G20 truce suspends Jan 1 tariff hike from 10% to 25% on ~$200B
US tariffs already cover ~$250B of Chinese exports ($50B at 25%, ~$200B at 10%)
Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou arrested Dec 1 on US extradition — firm-level targeting of China tech champion
China detained two Canadians (Kovrig, Spavor) Dec 10 — hostage/retaliation dynamic
Macro deceleration: Q3 GDP 6.5% (slowest since 2009), Nov IP growth 5.4% (lowest since 2009), export growth halved, yuan ~6% weaker on the year

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window; planned Jan 1 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended. Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
China detains Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor (widely viewed as retaliation for the Meng arrest).
